question: As of 18 October 2026, Indonesia will extend the halal certification requirement to a wide range of non-food products, including clothing, footwear, cosmetics and consumer goods, also imposing traceability requirements and Muslim supervisors on foreign companies.

These requirements are based on religious principles and risk becoming heavy trade barriers, forcing Italian and European companies to bear additional costs and adapt their production chains to enter the Indonesian market. This is happening as the European Union advances the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) with Indonesia, which should ensure reciprocity and the removal of trade barriers.
It is paradoxical that, as Europe opens up its markets, its businesses may face new religious and bureaucratic demands from trading partners. In the light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission not consider the imposition of religious certifications even on non‑food products to be an unjustified barrier to trade that is incompatible with the CEPA’s objectives of reciprocity and open markets?
Is the Commission prepared to suspend progress on the CEPA until it obtains binding guarantees from Indonesia against disproportionate requirements that would penalise European companies?
